prices.workload:
All hours are for 1× RTX 4090 (24 GB) with PyTorch AMP. For another GPU, divide by its rough speed relative to a 4090 on this kind of small-convnet training (my estimates, not measured): 3090 0.6×, L4 0.3×, L40S 0.9×, A100 1.1×, 5090 or RTX PRO 6000 1.4×, H100 1.8×, RTX 5060 Ti or Hetzner RTX PRO 4000 SFF about 0.4×.

Data
- S3OD: 139,981 image+mask pairs, 36.8 GB of parquet, 768-1,090 px. The dataset card is tagged MIT and its README is empty. Sources: https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/size?dataset=okupyn/s3od_dataset, https://huggingface.co/datasets/okupyn/s3od_dataset
- Your own photos: I assumed N = 20k. Resize them locally to at most 1600 px and strip EXIF (phone GPS data) before uploading. That is about 5 GB per 10k photos, or about 15 minutes at 50 Mbit/s upload.

Step 0, setup and data prep: 0.5-1 GPU-h. This covers pip installs, downloading S3OD from Hugging Face (a few minutes), converting it once to at most 1024 px files, and the upload.

Step 1, teacher pseudo-labels: InSPyReNet SwinB Plus Ultra at 1024 px in fp16, batched through a DataLoader, saving the soft alpha as 8-bit PNG.
- Throughput estimate: 10-30 images/s, central 15. The basis is BiRefNet, which uses the heavier Swin-L and runs at 17 FPS at 1024 px in fp16 on a 4090 (its README: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet/main/README.md). InSPyReNet is about 4× lighter on your CPU (10 s vs 40 s), so image decoding and PNG writing become the limit.
- Your photos only (20k): 0.2-0.6 h.
- S3OD plus your photos (160k): 1.5-4.5 h, central about 3 h.
- Each extra 10k photos adds 0.2-0.3 h. Flip test-time augmentation for cleaner labels doubles the time.
- This runs once and the labels are reused for every iteration.
- Labelling S3OD is optional because it ships with masks. But per NOTES.md those masks are almost binary (only 0.7% semi-transparent), so the teacher labels are what pass InSPyReNet's soft edges on to the student.

Step 2, student training: offline distillation on the stored teacher masks. Online distillation would run the teacher at every step and cost about 5-10× more.
- Student size: to hit 1-2 s on 4 CPU threads it needs about 5-10× fewer FLOPs than InSPyReNet, roughly 0.1-0.15 TFLOP per 1024 px image (ResNet-18 or MobileNet-class encoder with a U-Net/FPN decoder).
- Throughput: a training step costs about 3× the forward pass. At an effective 15-25 TFLOPS on a 4090 that gives about 80-120 images/s at 768 px and 180-250 images/s at 512 px. This needs at least 8-12 CPU cores for decoding and augmentation, or pre-resized data.
- One epoch over 160k images takes about 11-16 minutes at 512 px and 22-33 minutes at 768 px.
- 20 epochs at 512 px: 3.5-5 h.
- 40 epochs at 640 px (or 30 at 512 px plus 10 at 768 px): 10-14 h.
- 60 epochs at 768 px: 22-33 h.
- Each extra 10k photos adds about 7% to the training time.

Step 3, evaluation per run: 0.1-0.3 GPU-h. This means running the student and computing metrics on a held-out set, for example 2k S3OD images, 1-2k of your photos, and your test_syn, test_syn2 and test_clean sets. The CPU latency and ONNX/WASM checks run on your own PC for free.

Overhead: add 1-4 h per session for smoke tests and debugging. Start with a 15-minute benchmark of about 1,000 steps and replace my images/s figures with the measured ones before committing to a long run.

Totals per full run
- Lean: about 6 GPU-h. Teacher on your photos only, 20 epochs at 512 px.
- Typical: about 18 GPU-h. Teacher on S3OD plus your photos, 40 epochs at 640 px.
- Generous: about 45 GPU-h. N = 50k, flip augmentation, 60 epochs at 768 px.

Totals for 3 iterations (labels made once; training and evaluation three times)
- Lean: about 16 GPU-h.
- Typical: about 45 GPU-h.
- Generous: about 115 GPU-h.

- The same on RunPod Secure Cloud: about €45-55.
- Generous: €55-110.

Biggest risk: a GPU left running. A Secure 4090 forgotten over a weekend costs about €38. Have the training script stop the pod when it finishes (on RunPod: runpodctl stop pod $RUNPOD_POD_ID), and copy results to a network volume or your own PC first.

Pseudo-labelling your photos on their own costs only cents: about €0.10 per 10k photos.
prices.buy_advice:
Short version: rent for this project, and wait before buying a GPU PC.

- Your current PC is a 4th-gen Intel laptop with 11 GB RAM and no NVIDIA GPU. It can't take a GPU, so buying means a whole new PC.

VRAM needed
- Training the student at 512-768 px with AMP and batch 16-32 needs about 8-14 GB, so 16 GB is enough.
- Running the teacher at 1024 px needs about 3-6 GB. BiRefNet, which is heavier, needs 3.5 GB in fp16 according to its README.
- Fine-tuning a big model later needs 24 GB minimum, and 32-48 GB is comfortable. BiRefNet needs 23.5 GB on a 4090 with bf16 and compile at batch 2, and 36.5 GB or more without them. Rent for that kind of job.

Prices now
Because of the 2026 memory shortage, cards cost 1.5-3× their list price. PCGH (citing Reuters and TrendForce) expects no relief before 2027-28. German prices (NL is similar):
- RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB: about €620-650 on 31 Aug 2026; $800 in the US on 14 Nov.
- RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB: about €1,130 on 31 Aug; reportedly being discontinued.
- RTX 5080 16 GB: about €1,350 on 31 Aug. By early November it was 77% above list price globally, which is about €1,800.
- RTX 5090 32 GB: from €5,999 on 2 Oct, against a list price of €2,099. It reached $9,400 in the US in October.
- Used RTX 3090 24 GB: about $1,600. Used RTX 4090: about $3,400. Both are eBay US asking prices on 14 Nov.
- RAM: a 32 GB DDR5 kit costs over £400 in the UK (October).

My rough estimate for a complete PC (8-core CPU, 32 GB DDR5, 2 TB NVMe):
- With an RTX 5060 Ti: €1,700-2,300.
- With an RTX 5080: €3,000-3,500.
- With an RTX 5090: €7,000 or more.

Buying vs renting
- A 5060 Ti is about 0.4× as fast as a 4090, so a typical 18-hour run takes about 45 hours at home.
- At €0.32/kWh, a 250-300 W system costs €0.08-0.10 per hour in electricity. That is €0.20-0.25 per hour of 4090-equivalent work. Renting a community 4090 costs €0.31 per hour.
- Even a home 4090 or 5090 uses about €0.16-0.19 of electricity per 4090-hour of work.
- So you save at most about €0.05-0.15 per training hour. A €2,000 PC would never pay for itself through saved rent.

When buying does make sense
- You will run GPU jobs on most days for years.
- Your photos must not leave the house. Pseudo-labelling at home on the CPU is also free: about 28 hours per 10k photos.
- You want to iterate without any setup.

If you do buy:
- Choose NVIDIA, for CUDA, PyTorch and onnxruntime-gpu.
- Get at least 16 GB VRAM. The RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB is the value pick; skip 8 GB cards.
- 32-64 GB RAM, at least 8 CPU cores for data loading, and 2 TB NVMe.
- Only pay for 24-32 GB if you will fine-tune the teacher at home.
- Ideally wait until prices drop back towards list price (5090 €2,099, 5080 €1,059).

Two practical notes
- Even a cheap GPU or a recent integrated GPU is enough to test the browser WebGPU path. NOTES.md marks it as untested because there is no GPU.
- Measure the CPU target (1-2 s on 4 threads) on a CPU-only PC like your current one, not on the GPU machine.

Renting is better for this one-off project (tens of euros), for anything that needs more than 16-24 GB, for parallel experiments, and for as long as buy prices are 2-3× list price.

students.name: Student A: IS-Net architecture (DIS ISNetDIS, full width), trained from random init and distilled
students.code_licence: Apache-2.0. The xuebinqin/DIS README says 'Our code and evaluation metric use Apache License 2.0' (https://github.com/xuebinqin/DIS). The architecture is in IS-Net/models/isnet.py (https://github.com/xuebinqin/DIS/blob/main/IS-Net/models/isnet.py). Keep the Apache notice and change the heads to return logits.
students.weights_licence: No pretrained weights are needed: the model starts from random init with no backbone. U2-Net/IS-Net are built to train from scratch (arXiv 2005.09007 abstract: 'train a deep network from scratch without using backbones from image classification tasks'). The DIS training script loads no weights (restore_model and gt_encoder_model are empty: https://github.com/xuebinqin/DIS/blob/main/IS-Net/train_valid_inference_main.py). The resulting weights belong to the owner. The training data is: (1) S3OD, licence field 'mit' (https://huggingface.co/datasets/okupyn/s3od_dataset); its images come from FLUX.1-Krea-dev, and FLUX.1 [dev] Non-Commercial License v1.1.2 section 2(d) says 'You may use Output for any purpose (including for commercial purposes)' (https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-Krea-dev/blob/main/LICENSE.md); (2) the owner's own photos; (3) labels from teachers whose weights are MIT (BiRefNet general, InSPyReNet Plus Ultra). Do NOT initialise from isnet-general-use.pth or u2net.pth (published without a weight licence) or from RMBG-1.4 (non-commercial).
students.cpu_speed_estimate: Measured on the owner's PC: i7-4700MQ Haswell, onnxruntime 1.32 CPU, fp32, 4 threads, random weights, model inference only, median of 5 runs, with some background load. Results: 1.60 s at 1024 px and 0.84 s at 768 px; 159.6 GMACs at 1024 px; ONNX file 176 MB. Calibration: the real models/isnet-general.onnx took 1.63 s in the same conditions. In bench, isnet-general and RMBG-1.4 (same graph) take 1.48 s and 1.65 s per photo including pre- and post-processing, with a peak of about 0.9 GB RAM. Expect about 1.5-1.8 s per photo end to end, about 6x faster than the InSPyReNet ONNX (10 s).
students.wasm_ok: Yes, already shown in practice. The graph uses the same ops as RMBG-1.4, which already runs in the AlphaMaker web app on WASM (about 5-6 s per photo in Firefox, per README) and on WebGPU. It uses only Conv (including dilated), MaxPool(ceil_mode), Resize (bilinear), Concat, Add, Relu and Sigmoid. The ORT docs say 'All ONNX operators are supported by WASM' (https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/tutorials/web/). Peak memory is about 1 GB, well under the 4 GB WASM limit. Downside: a 176 MB fp32 download (RMBG-1.4 is 168 MB). fp16 or int8 for a smaller download is untested in the browser.
students.why: This is the safest bet for quality within 1-2 s. RMBG-1.4 uses this same graph and has the best clean-object edges in the owner's benchmark (edge-MAE 0.066 on DIS-VD), yet it scores 0.19 on busy test_syn. So the architecture can produce sharp edges, and the training data decides the rest; distilling on S3OD plus the owner's photos targets exactly that. The decoder works at high resolution (stage1/stage1d run at 512x512 with 64 channels for a 1024 input), and its six side outputs give deep supervision that suits soft-target distillation. There is no backbone, so the ImageNet licence question does not arise. The owner's bench and web code already handle this graph (HALF normalisation). The network is fully convolutional, so training at several scales makes 768 px (0.84 s) usable as a fast mode.

students.name: Student B: MobileNetV4-Conv-Medium U-Net (timm encoder, features_only) with a depthwise-separable decoder, global context and a full-resolution head, trained from random init
students.code_licence: Apache-2.0 for the encoder code: the timm README says 'The code here is licensed Apache 2.0' (https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models). The decoder and head are the owner's own code (about 40 lines). Avoid segmentation_models_pytorch: it is MIT, but its README says 'some files are subject to other licenses ... especially for commercial use' (https://github.com/qubvel-org/segmentation_models.pytorch). For example, its SegFormer/MiT encoders fall under the NVIDIA Source Code License, 'only may be used ... non-commercially' (https://github.com/NVlabs/SegFormer/blob/master/LICENSE).
students.weights_licence: None if trained from scratch, which is recommended. The optional timm ImageNet-1k init is not provably safe for commercial use. Its model card (mobilenetv4_conv_medium.e500_r256_in1k) says 'License: apache-2.0' and 'Trained on ImageNet-1k by Ross Wightman' (https://huggingface.co/timm/mobilenetv4_conv_medium.e500_r256_in1k). But the timm README says 'ImageNet was released for non-commercial research purposes only', 'one should assume that the original dataset license applies to the weights', and recommends seeking legal advice before commercial use. torchvision says pre-trained models 'may have their own licenses or terms and conditions derived from the dataset used for training' (https://docs.pytorch.org/vision/stable/models.html). The ImageNet terms say 'Researcher shall use the Database only for non-commercial research and educational purposes' (https://huggingface.co/datasets/ILSVRC/imagenet-1k). The same applies to every ImageNet-1k backbone (timm EfficientNet-B0 card apache-2.0, RepViT repo Apache-2.0, ConvNeXt-pico card apache-2.0, all trained on ImageNet-1k). No ruling settles whether weights inherit the dataset's terms, so under the owner's rule they should not be shipped.

That is about 4.4x faster than Student A. In the browser on WASM, estimate about 1-1.5 s. This uses the owner's own native-to-Firefox ratio of about 3x (InSPyReNet 10 s native vs 29 s in Firefox, RMBG-1.4 1.65 s vs 5-6 s).
students.wasm_ok: Yes, expected. The graph uses only Conv, depthwise Conv, Relu, Resize, Concat, ReduceMean, Add and Sigmoid: no HardSwish, SiLU or attention. All of these are supported by WASM. 29 MB fits easily. Whether WebGPU runs the exported graph still needs confirming with tests/web/run_browser_smoke.sh.
students.why: This is the fastest candidate that still keeps a stride-2 skip connection, a global-pooling context term at stride 32, and a full-resolution refinement head (decoder at 8 channels, upsampled, concatenated with RGB, then two 3x3 convs). It is a small download for the web, and the encoder has enough capacity for busy scenes. Alternatives measured with the same decoder at 1024 px: MobileNetV3-L 0.30 s (3.2M params), MobileNetV4-small 0.19 s (1.5M, probably too weak), EfficientNet-B0 0.55 s (SiLU and SE layers are slow on this CPU despite only 11 GMACs), RepViT-M0.9 0.55 s, ConvNeXt-pico 0.59 s, ResNet-18 0.53 s. None is faster at equal capacity, and all have the same ImageNet-weights problem. If its edges fall short: widen the head to 16 channels (about +0.1 s), or use IS-Net at half width with Student A's code (measured 11.0M params, 40 GMACs, 0.52 s at 1024 px, 0.27 s at 768 px).

design.recipe:
One training script with a flag --arch isnet|mnv4m. Both students use the same data, labels and losses, and both start from random init.

1. DATA AND SPLIT
- S3OD (okupyn/s3od_dataset, 139,981 rows, 36.8 GB, columns image/mask/image_id/category/caption). Pin the dataset revision.
- Remove the 120 image_ids used in ~/claude/AlphaMaker/data/test_syn and data/test_syn2 (file names syn_<image_id>.jpg). Also remove any row whose caption matches a test caption.
- Hold out 2,000 random rows as the validation set. About 137.8k rows remain for training.
- Never add DIS5K or PPM-100: they are non-commercial and they are the test_clean* sets.
- Owner photos: remove near-duplicates with a perceptual hash and keep at most 5 shots per item. Split by item: 90% train, 10% validation, so no item is in both.
- From the held-out items, hand-correct 100 photos as a new test set 'test_eigen'. Start from the BiRefNet mask and fix it with the eraser/restore brush in the AlphaMaker web editor.
- Pre-resize everything once to 1024x1024 square with PIL BILINEAR, exactly like bench.predict_onnx and core. Store JPEG q95 for images and PNG for labels. This keeps decoding 12 MP photos from slowing training down.
- Each batch is about 60% S3OD and 40% owner photos (oversample the owner photos if there are fewer).

2. TEACHERS, ENSEMBLE AND LABEL FILTERING (offline, once, on the GPU)
- Teachers: BiRefNet general (pt-birefnet-general, MIT) at 1024 as the main target, and InSPyReNet Plus Ultra (pinned ONNX sha256 c108dd92..., MIT) at 1024 as a second opinion.
- Owner photos: run both teachers, each with horizontal-flip test-time augmentation (average the flipped-back result). S3OD: run BiRefNet only, without the flip; the S3OD mask serves as the second opinion.
- Why BiRefNet is the target, measured on the owner's saved predictions for test_syn + test_syn2 (120 images):
  - InSPyReNet: edge 0.133, 10 misses. BiRefNet: edge 0.114, 12 misses. 50/50 mean: edge 0.122, 10 misses.
  - Keeping only images where the teachers agree (IoU of BiRefNet>0.5 vs InSPyReNet>0.5 at least 0.90) keeps 104 of 120. On those, BiRefNet alone scores edge 0.100, MAE 0.0103, 4 misses, and blending InSPyReNet in is worse (0.109 at 50/50). The 16 dropped images have edge about 0.21.
- Owner photos: keep if teacher agreement is at least 0.90 and the flip-consistency IoU is at least 0.95. Otherwise send the photo to a manual-correction queue; these busy scenes are worth the most. Corrected photos go back in with sample weight 2, or else they are dropped.
- S3OD: if IoU(BiRefNet, S3OD mask) is at least 0.90, the target is BiRefNet's soft alpha. Otherwise the target is the S3OD mask, which is hard (S3OD itself already passed flip-IoU of at least 0.8, Gemma-3 checks and at most 5 components, removing 6.8%: arXiv 2510.21605).
- All images: drop the label if the foreground covers less than 0.3% or more than 95% of the image, or has more than 5 large components.
- Store targets as uint8 PNG soft alpha at 1024. Keep a provenance log: dataset revision, teacher hashes and script commit.

3. INPUT
- RGB, the full photo square-resized, normalised with mean 0.5 and std 1.0 (IS-Net style, the bench 'HALF' setting).
- The model outputs a logit at full resolution.
- Student A: phase 1 at 768 crops, phase 2 at 1024, with 20% of phase-2 batches at 768 so that 768 works as a fast mode. RMBG-1.4 broke at 768 because it was trained only at 1024.
- Student B: 1024 throughout, with 20% of batches at 768.

4. AUGMENTATIONS (on the fly; the mask follows only the geometric ones)
- Geometric: RandomResizedCrop with scale 0.35-1.0 and aspect ratio 0.75-1.33; horizontal flip p=0.5; rotation of plus or minus 8 degrees with p=0.2; no vertical flip.
- Synthetic backgrounds, p=0.35: estimate the foreground with AlphaMaker's blur-fusion, then composite I = aF + (1-a)B.
  - Plain backgrounds (60%): uniform white, grey, beige, black or pastel; a linear or radial gradient of plus or minus 15%; vignette; noise with sigma 1-4/255; blurred-noise 'fabric' texture; a soft contact shadow (alpha offset 5-30 px, blur 15-60 px, opacity 0.2-0.5). The label is still the object alpha only.
  - Busy backgrounds (40%): another training photo, randomly cropped, blurred with sigma 0-4 for depth of field, with the object placed at 40-90% of the frame height.
- Lighting and colour (p=0.8, applied after compositing):
  - white-balance gains: R and B in 0.65-1.35, G in 0.9-1.1 (tungsten and fluorescent casts);
  - exposure x0.35-1.6 in linear light; gamma 0.7-1.4; contrast 0.6-1.15; saturation 0.5-1.3;
  - a low-frequency lamp-falloff field (2-4 Gaussian blobs, plus or minus 40%), p=0.3; a hard shadow polygon, p=0.1;
  - Poisson-Gaussian noise, stronger when darkened, p=0.5; JPEG quality 40-95, p=0.5; blur of at most 1.5 px, p=0.2; downscale-upscale by x0.4-1, p=0.3.

5. LOSSES
- Use BCEWithLogits. IS-Net's BCELoss on sigmoid outputs is not safe under autocast.
- t is the soft target. The edge band B is (0.02 < t < 0.98) plus an 8 px band around the contour of t>0.5, the same zone as bench.metrics. The pixel weight is w = 1 + 4B.
- Final output: L = weighted BCE + weighted soft IoU + 0.5(1 - SSIM with an 11x11 window) + 1.0 L1(p,t) inside B + 0.5 L1 between the Sobel gradients of p and t inside B. BCE+IoU+SSIM is BASNet's hybrid loss; the L1 and gradient terms are matting-style.
- Side outputs (IS-Net d2-d6; auxiliary heads at /4 and /8 for Student B): BCE + IoU against the area-downsampled t, weight 0.4 each.
- This is response-only distillation: the teachers' soft alphas are the targets, with no feature distillation.

6. OPTIMISER, SCHEDULE AND BATCH
- Student A: AdamW lr 1e-3 (IS-Net's own setting was Adam lr 1e-3, batch 8, 1024 px, horizontal flip only), weight decay 1e-4, 2k warmup steps, cosine to 1e-6.
  - Phase 1: batch 16 at 768 for 8 epochs. Phase 2: batch 8 at 1024 for 4 epochs.
  - About 150k steps, about 1.8M samples.
  - bf16 autocast, channels_last, torch.compile, gradient clipping at 1.0, EMA 0.9995 (evaluate the EMA weights).
  - About 1 GB of activations per sample at 1024, so it fits in 24 GB.
- Student B: AdamW lr 2e-3, weight decay 0.05, batch 32 at 1024, 3k warmup steps, cosine, 25 epochs (about 3.7M samples), EMA 0.9995. Use at least 8 vCPU for data loading.
- Validate each epoch on the S3OD validation rows and the owner's validation items (edge-MAE, MAE, misses with IoU<0.8). Keep the best EMA checkpoint, and stop after 3 epochs without improvement.

7. EXPORT
- Wrap the model so it outputs only the final full-resolution logit. Export with torch.onnx.export at opset 17: one export with a fixed 1x3x1024x1024 input (like the InSPyReNet ONNX, simplest for WebGPU) and one with dynamic H/W in multiples of 32.
- Check parity: ORT vs PyTorch max |difference| below 1e-3 on 20 photos.
- Register the model in the owner's code as (path, 1024, HALF, 'sigmoid'), not 'minmax'.
- int8: run onnxruntime.quantization preprocess, then quantize_static with QDQ, per_channel=True and S8S8 (the ORT default). Set reduce_range=True for AVX2 CPUs without VNNI such as the i7-4700MQ (ORT docs). Calibrate on 300 training images with percentile or entropy calibration. Exclude the first conv, side1/the full-resolution head and the Sigmoid.
- Ship int8 only if edge-MAE on test_syn2 rises by no more than 0.003 AND it is actually faster on the i7. ORT warns that old CPUs can be slower, and the owner's dynamic-int8 InSPyReNet took 16.2 s vs 10.3 s. Otherwise ship fp32, and try fp16 weights only as a smaller web download.
- Optionally convert to .ort format for the web.

8. EVALUATION
- Run bench/bench.py, with the student added as a model, on:
  - test_syn and test_syn2 (from S3OD, so in-distribution for the student and optimistic);
  - test_clean and test_clean2 (DIS-VD + PPM-100: clean for the student, contaminated for InSPyReNet);
  - the studio_study plain backgrounds;
  - test_eigen.
- Report edge-MAE, MAE, IoU, misses, seconds per photo on the i7 with 4 threads, and peak RAM. In the browser: tests/web/run_browser_smoke.sh plus timing in Firefox on WASM.
- Ship gate on syn, syn2 and test_eigen: edge-MAE no worse than InSPyReNet's (0.13 on syn), misses at most InSPyReNet's +2, CPU time at most 2 s. Look at a montage of the 10 worst photos.

9. GPU TIME AND COST
- RunPod list prices (https://www.runpod.io/pricing): RTX 4090 $0.34/h community or $0.89/h secure; L40S $0.79/$1.09; A100 80GB $1.19-2.19.
- Estimate:
  - labelling: about 7-9 GPU-hours (BiRefNet at roughly 6-8 images/s);
  - Student A: 12-20 GPU-hours (25-45 samples/s);
  - Student B: 7-12 GPU-hours;
  - pilots and evaluation: about 10 GPU-hours.
- Total about 35-50 GPU-hours on a 4090, roughly $15-45, plus a few dollars for an 80 GB storage volume. Budget about EUR 100-150 to cover a pilot and one failed run.
- A 24-32 GB GPU PC runs the same recipe locally.
design.risks:
1. Quality is unproven: no student has been trained yet. A student can at best approach its teacher (BiRefNet edge-MAE about 0.114 on the busy sets). Expect roughly 0.12-0.15 for A and worse for B. The labels dropped by the filter (about 13%) are exactly the busy scenes, so correcting them by hand pays off.

2. Evaluation bias: test_syn and test_syn2 are S3OD photos, which is in-distribution for the student. That flatters the student compared with InSPyReNet. Decide on test_clean*, studio_study and test_eigen. The teacher's DIS-VD scores are contaminated; the student's are not. test_eigen starts from BiRefNet masks, which favours BiRefNet's style slightly.

3. Licences:
(a) Teacher training data. InSPyReNet Plus Ultra was trained on DUTS, DIS5K including VD/TE, HRSOD, UHRSD, MSRA-10K, HKU-IS and others (https://github.com/plemeri/InSPyReNet/blob/main/docs/model_zoo.md). BiRefNet general was trained on DIS5K TR+TE, P3M and others. Many of these are research-only datasets. Both sets of weights carry an explicit MIT licence. The student inherits the same residual risk the owner has already accepted for these teachers.
(b) S3OD. The licence field says MIT, but the README is empty. The images come from FLUX-Krea, whose licence (FLUX.1 [dev] Non-Commercial v1.1.2, section 2(d)) allows commercial use of outputs. It only forbids using outputs to train a model that competes with FLUX, and a segmenter does not. The masks were made with DINOv3 ViT-L features (arXiv 2510.21605). The DINOv3 licence restricts how DINO Materials are used (for example military use) but says nothing about outputs (https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov3/blob/main/LICENSE.md). The residual risk is low. To remove it entirely, do not use the S3OD masks: train on teacher labels only and gate with InSPyReNet instead.
(c) Never initialise from isnet-general-use.pth or u2net.pth (no weight licence), RMBG-1.4 (non-commercial), S3OD's own models (DINOv3 licence), or timm/torchvision ImageNet weights (timm's author says to assume ImageNet's non-commercial terms apply). Train from scratch only.

4. Student B is trained from scratch without ImageNet and may handle busy scenes less well. Fallback: IS-Net at half width (0.52 s), or Student A at 768 px (0.84 s).

5. Speed figures: random weights, model inference only, with background load on the i7-4700MQ. The real isnet-general.onnx took 1.63 s in the same conditions vs 1.48 s in bench. Add 0.1-0.3 s of pre- and post-processing for a 12 MP photo. WASM is about 3x slower than native. Student A's 176 MB download is large for the web, and fp16/int8 are unproven in the browser. int8 may not be faster on Haswell.

6. GPU throughput figures are estimates and could be off by 2x. Measure the first 15 minutes of each job and extrapolate. Data loading can become the bottleneck for Student B.

7. Privacy: the owner's photos would sit on a third-party GPU. Community-cloud hosts are third parties, so use secure cloud, preferably in the EU, and delete the storage volume afterwards.

8. Rejected:
- SegFormer/MiT: NVIDIA licence, non-commercial only.
- RobustVideoMatting: GPL-3.0.
- InSPyReNet with Res2Net50: the timm card says 'License: unknown' (https://huggingface.co/timm/res2net50_26w_4s.in1k), and it is heavy.
- PP-LiteSeg (PaddleSeg, Apache-2.0) and BiSeNet (MIT): semantic-segmentation heads at 1/8 resolution give weak edges, their released weights are trained on Cityscapes/CamVid/COCO-Stuff, and PP-LiteSeg needs the Paddle toolchain.
- MODNet (Apache-2.0 code and models): portrait-only; the owner measured hair edges of 0.127 and it is unusable on objects.
- U-2-Net(-p) at 320 px: edges 2.5x worse (measured).

Not checked: student quality (nothing was trained), real GPU throughput, WebGPU support of Student B's graph, fp16/int8 in the browser, prices other than RunPod. This is not legal advice.

colour.current_code_review:
Scope: ~/Marktplaats/sellyourshit-3.5/marktplaats_suite/image_enhancer.py (104 lines). It is called through fotoverwerking.py L224-226 (_verbeter_kleur -> auto_enhance(pad, pad), which overwrites the prepared JPEG) from step 2 of maak_versies (L386-397). That is BEFORE background removal (L400-415). I measured it on the owner's own photos: 7 Fairphone-6 shots of a stein (~/.local/share/marktplaats-suite/input vs output) and 4 Galaxy-XCover7 shots of a chair from nieuw_werkmap/product_ingsl59e, re-enhanced in the scratchpad.

1. There is no white balance at all, and L27 ImageEnhance.Color(1.20) boosts saturation evenly, so colour casts get stronger. The stein table goes from b* +6.8 to +10.0 (+9.8 to +14.4 on the worst shot). The goal is the reverse.
2. The gains are fixed and do not adapt: L22 Contrast 1.15, L27 Color 1.20, L32 Brightness 1.08, L37-43 UnsharpMask (radius 1.5, 130%, threshold 3) and L56 CLAHE (clip 2.0, 8x8). A dark photo, a bright photo and an already good photo all get the same treatment. There is no metering, no strength control and no preview.
3. Tones get crushed and clipped:
   - L22: Pillow's Contrast pivots on the image's mean grey.
   - L32: Brightness is a plain multiply.
   - Every PIL step re-quantises and clips to uint8.
   Measured: on the product region, the 1st percentile of L* drops from 8.2 to 1.5 (steins) and from 11.7 to 1.2 (chairs). Clipped pixels on the stein go from 0.14% to 2.0% of the image. On the chair shoot with a white backdrop they go from 7.7% to 28%, and clipping on the chair itself goes from 0.01% to 0.47%.
4. L53-60 applies CLAHE to the L channel of 8-bit Lab on every photo. Plain and white backgrounds come out mottled: the white table turns into dirty yellow-grey blotches. Wood grain, scratches and JPEG noise are amplified. The a/b channels are left alone, so chroma no longer matches the new lightness.
5. L37-43 sharpens in RGB before CLAHE, so CLAHE amplifies the halos and the chroma noise. It also sharpens before AlphaMaker, so the halos end up in the cutout edge. The radius does not depend on the output size.
6. Order: enhancement (fotoverwerking.py L393-397) runs before AlphaMaker (L400-415). So it cannot use the product mask (no keeping the background white, no vibrance or sharpening on the product only), and the segmenter receives an image already processed by CLAHE and sharpening.
7. Colour management: _bereid_voor keeps the ICC profile (fotoverwerking.py L217, L221) and the versions copy it (L447, L451). But auto_enhance reads with cv2.imread and saves without icc_profile (L9, L67-68). So when colour enhancement is on, iPhone Display-P3 photos are silently treated as sRGB. It also adds a third JPEG generation with 4:2:0 subsampling (prep q95, then enhance q95, then version q95).
8. Failures are silent: L9-11 just return when cv2.imread fails. OpenCV never added wide-character paths on Windows (https://github.com/opencv/opencv/issues/4292 was closed in 2020 with the advice to use imdecode). maak_versies (L393-397) then reports nothing and the photo is simply not enhanced.
9. Dependency check: L6 imports tqdm at module level, and heeft_kleurverbetering (fotoverwerking.py L136-137) requires tqdm, although only the CLI loop (L79) uses it. Without tqdm the GUI disables the option with a tooltip that blames opencv (productmanager.py L2847-2849).
10. Speed is not the problem: about 0.3 s per 3.1 MP including JPEG input and output (measured), against about 10 s for InSPyReNet.

Verdict: on these photos the current output is worse than the original (stronger cast, crushed shadows, blown backdrop, blotchy background). Replace it rather than tune it. The CLI part (L71-104) can stay as a thin wrapper.

colour.recommendation:
VERDICT: ship a classical, mask-aware pipeline now. It is commercially clean: your own code plus numpy (BSD), OpenCV (Apache-2.0) and Pillow (MIT-CMU), with no weights and no training data. No published pretrained enhancement model is commercially usable: FiveK and PPR10K are research-only, Zero-DCE and Afifi's WB models are non-commercial, and CSRNet has no licence. A learned model is an optional phase 2, trained on the owner's own data.

PIPELINE
A prototype is at (lokaal pad) Original | current | proposed: (lokaal pad) The scratchpad can be wiped on reboot.

0. Ingest (_bereid_voor):
   - EXIF transpose, embedded ICC converted to sRGB with ImageCms, optional 50% resize.
   - Read with PIL, never cv2.imread.
   - Keep the prep in memory or as PNG, so only one JPEG generation remains.

1. Order:
   - When any background option is on: run AlphaMaker on the UNENHANCED prep.
   - Then, per photo, P = params(prep, alpha) and apply(prep, P, alpha) for the photo versions.
   - Apply the same P to the cutout's RGB (blur-fusion foreground colours, alpha as mask) before 'transparant', 'wit' and 'custom'.
   - With no background option: params(prep, None) in step 2, as now.

2. Statistics: computed on a 512 px thumbnail (INTER_AREA), in linear light (256-entry sRGB-to-linear LUT). Valid pixels: max channel < 0.92 and Y > 0.01.

3. White balance:
   - Reference ring = dilate(alpha>0.5, 41 px) minus dilate(alpha>0.5, 9 px) at 512 px, valid pixels only; it must cover at least 5% of the image. This is the surface next to the product, lit by the same light. Fallback: eroded background (alpha < 0.05).
   - Illuminant = mean of the brighter half of the reference. Accept it if the median Y is above 0.25, it lies within 0.06 log-chroma of the Planckian candidates (2700-10000 K x tint 0.97-1.03, Kang et al. 2002 locus) and |log r/g| and |log b/g| are below 0.8. Snap it to the nearest candidate and apply it at full strength.
   - Otherwise use grey-pixel voting over 3500-10000 K x 5 tints. Each candidate scores the sum of sqrt(Y) over pixels with max(|dlog r/g|, |dlog b/g|) < 0.05; background pixels count 3x, and the neutral candidate gets a 1.15x prior. Strength k = clip((conf-0.05)/0.2, 0.3, 1).
   - gains = (1/illuminant)^k, normalised to keep luminance. Fade to no correction as a pixel's max channel goes from 0.9 to 1.0, so clipped whites stay white.
   - Listing: use the median reference-backed illuminant for all photos of one product (same light), so a listing's photos match.

4. Exposure:
   - Bright neutral background (more than 5% of the image, median Y above 0.3): background median goes to 0.86 linear (about L* 94, sRGB about 240).
   - Otherwise: image 99th percentile goes to 0.88.
   - Clamp the gain to 0.8-2.2 (about -0.3 to +1.1 EV).
   - Add a cap from the product's 98th percentile so speculars do not grow.

5. Shadows: fast guided filter on log2 Y at 512 px (r = 10 px, eps = 0.25 stop^2). Lift = clip(0.30*(log2 0.18 - base), 0, 0.8) EV, with the coefficients a and b upsampled bilinearly and applied to full-resolution log Y (no halos).

6. Tone curve:
   - Black point = min(0.2nd percentile, 0.01).
   - Soft shoulder with knee 0.80: above it, y -> k + (1-k)(1 - e^(-(y-k)/(1-k))).
   - Scale RGB by Y'/Y to keep hue.
   - Desaturate out-of-gamut pixels toward Y' instead of clipping each channel.

7. Vibrance in CIELAB: C' = C*(1+0.20*alpha*(1-min(C/60,1))^2). This touches the product only, so the background stays neutral.

8. Sharpening, last and at output size: unsharp mask on L*, sigma = max(0.7, long side/2000), amount 0.6, threshold 1 L*, weighted by alpha.

9. Output: JPEG q92-95 with subsampling=0, sRGB.

10. UI: a strength slider (0-100%, default 100) that scales every step, plus a before/after toggle. Cache P per photo so a re-render is instant.

CPU COST (measured on this PC, OpenCV limited to 4 threads)
- 3.1 MP: params 90 ms + apply about 0.5 s (current enhancer: 0.3 s).
- 12.5 MP: 1.95 s and about 410 MB numpy peak when processed in 768-row stripes, against 4.7 s and 1.4 GB in one piece. Use stripes above 4 MP.
- Either way it is negligible next to AlphaMaker's 10 s.

RESULTS ON THE OWNER'S PHOTOS (11 photos, 2 shoots; stein masks are rough U-2-Net test masks)
- Steins:
  - Table L* 76-82 goes to 93-94.
  - Table b* +6.8..+8.5 goes to +1.6..+2.7 on 4 of 7 photos; the other 3 improve less (+5.0/+4.8/+8.2).
  - The product's dark end (1st-percentile L*) improves from 8.2 to 10.8; the current enhancer crushes it to 1.5.
  - Specular pixels on the product go from 0.22% to 1.3%, which the step-4 cap addresses.
- Chairs:
  - Backdrop L* 84-92 goes to 95-97.5, with |a*| and |b*| <= 1.4.
  - Chair highlight clipping is 0.16%, against 0.47% with the current enhancer.
- Synthetic casts:
  - 4000-10000 K: corrected to |b*| <= 3.
  - 2700-3000 K with the red channel near clipping: only partly corrected (b* +9..+26 left) — a known limit.

CODE CHANGES (smallest)
- image_enhancer.py: replace auto_enhance with params(rgb8, alpha=None, strength=1.0) and apply(rgb8, P, alpha=None) (about 150 lines). Keep auto_enhance(src, dst) as a CLI wrapper. Drop the module-level tqdm import.
- fotoverwerking.py:
  - heeft_kleurverbetering checks only cv2 and numpy.
  - Add the ICC conversion in _bereid_voor.
  - Move enhancement after verwijder_achtergrond when a background option is on, and apply the listing-wide white balance.
- pyproject: switch to opencv-python-headless. Non-headless Linux wheels bundle Qt5 under LGPLv3 (https://github.com/opencv/opencv-python), which is the same Qt the helper already works around by stripping QT_* variables.
- Self-checks (assert-based, like refine.py):
  - A grey card under 4000/8000 K comes out with |b*| <= 3.
  - strength=0 changes nothing beyond 1 level.
  - The tone LUT is monotonic.
  - A white background comes out at L* >= 92.
  - No NaN.

EVALUATION ON THE OWNER'S PHOTOS
1. Test set: 150-300 photos from about 40 listings, stratified by:
   - light: window, warm LED/tungsten, mixed, flash, dim;
   - background: white, cream, wood/coloured, busy;
   - product: white, black, saturated, metal/glass.
   About 20 shots should include a grey card or white paper next to the product.
2. Scripted metrics, using AlphaMaker masks:
   - grey card angular error (median <= 3 deg) or white-paper |a*|,|b*| <= 3;
   - ring/background L* 90-97 and chroma <= 3;
   - added clipping inside the product <= 0.5 percentage points;
   - product 1st-percentile L* not lower than the original;
   - spread (std) of product a*/b* across a listing lower than in the originals;
   - <= 1 s and <= 500 MB per 3 MP on the slowest target PC.
3. Blind, randomised side-by-side test (small GTK or HTML page) comparing the new output with:
   - the original;
   - the current enhancer;
   - Google Photos 'Enhance', which the owner applies on the phone to about 50 of the same photos. Use these only as an evaluation reference, never as training data. Google does not document Enhance beyond 'ML suggestions that apply brightness, contrast...' (https://blog.google/products/photos/new-helpful-editor/).
   Targets: win at least 80% against the current enhancer and at least 50% (parity) against Google Photos, and be judged worse than the original in at most 5% of photos. Tune the six knobs (WB strength, exposure targets 0.86/0.88, shadows 0.30, vibrance 0.20, sharpening 0.6, gain cap) on one half of the set and report on the other half.
4. Freeze the set and the metrics script, and rerun them on every change.

PHASE 2 (optional, on the rented GPU)
- Model: a tiny CNN (0.3-1M parameters, trained from scratch to avoid ImageNet terms). Input: a 256 px thumbnail plus a mask channel. Output: the pipeline's parameters (illuminant, EV, shadows, vibrance, black point); optionally a 3D-LUT head (Zeng et al. code is Apache-2.0).
- Deployment: ONNX of about 1-3 MB, about 5-20 ms on CPU, also usable with onnxruntime-web. The classical renderer stays in place, so the model cannot invent detail.
- Data:
  - slider values the owner logs when adjusting photos in the app;
  - synthetic pairs: the owner's approved photos (plus S3OD, MIT; beware of FLUX colour grading) degraded with the MIT WB augmenter or Planckian gains, +/-1.5 EV and contrast/gamma changes.
- Training cost: minutes to about one GPU-hour.
- Ship it only if it beats the classical pipeline in the same blind test (at least 55%) without raising the 'worse than original' rate.

SOURCES
- FiveK licence: https://data.csail.mit.edu/graphics/fivek/legal/LicenseAdobe.txt and https://data.csail.mit.edu/graphics/fivek/legal/LicenseAdobeMIT.txt
- PPR10K: https://github.com/csjliang/PPR10K
- Other licences: as cited in each method entry.
- Google Photos editing help: https://support.google.com/photos/answer/6128850

SKIPPED / RISKS
- Patents were not checked.
- No Google Photos outputs were compared here.
- Only 11 owner photos were tested.
- A cream or coloured background will be neutralised (by design; strength slider).

6. The other backbones match the claim:

   - https://huggingface.co/timm/convnext_pico.d1_in1k: apache-2.0, "Trained in timm on ImageNet-1k by Ross Wightman".
   - RepViT: the LICENSE is Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/THU-MIG/RepViT/blob/main/LICENSE) and the README says "Models are trained on ImageNet-1K".

8. The SegFormer LICENSE (https://github.com/NVlabs/SegFormer/blob/master/LICENSE) is titled "NVIDIA Source Code License for SegFormer". Clause 3.3 reads "The Work and any derivative works thereof only may be used or intended for use non-commercially". It defines non-commercially as "for research or evaluation purposes only".

9. "No ruling" is not refuted. Searches found no ruling on whether a dataset's licence or contract terms pass to trained weights. The closest case is Getty v Stability AI, on whether weights are "infringing copies". The UK Court of Appeal heard it in November 2026, and judgment is expected in spring or summer 2027. It is about copyright, not dataset terms (https://www.bclplaw.com/en-US/events-insights-news/key-ai-appeal-court-hearing-getty-v-stability-ai-flags-ai-model-training-and-use-conflicts-and-uk-v-eu-v-us-differences.html).
verdict.corrections:
The claim holds. Four caveats should be added.

1. Random init only removes the ImageNet starting weights. The student still learns from the teacher's pseudo-labels, and the teacher has the same problem the owner's rule targets:
   - InSPyReNet Plus Ultra uses `pretrained: True` with a SwinB backbone loaded from `swin_base_patch4_window12_384_22kto1k.pth`, which is ImageNet-22k pretrained and ImageNet-1k fine-tuned (https://github.com/plemeri/InSPyReNet/blob/main/lib/backbones/SwinTransformer.py).
   - It is trained on DIS-TR plus DIS-VD and DIS-TE1 to TE4, all from DIS5K, along with DUTS, HRSOD and other sets (https://github.com/plemeri/InSPyReNet/blob/main/configs/extra_dataset/Plus_Ultra.yaml). DIS5K is the reason IS-Net was rejected.
   - So under the owner's own rule, the teacher and any student distilled from it carry the same open question. Using ImageNet init would add no new kind of risk.
   - The claim's "weights: None" should read: "no third-party starting weights; the student's training sources are S3OD plus the teacher's outputs."

2. A licence is not a patent clearance. Google LLC holds US11734545B2, "Highly efficient convolutional neural networks" (https://patents.google.com/patent/US11734545B2/en).
   - It covers inverted residual blocks: an expansion convolution, a linear bottleneck, and a shortcut between bottlenecks. It is active, with an estimated expiry of 2042-01-03.
   - Its continuations US11823024B2 and US12547878B2 are active, and US20260154533A1 is pending.
   - timm's UniversalInvertedResidual has exactly those parts: a `pw_exp` expansion, a `pw_proj` with `apply_act=False` (linear), and a skip when input and output channels match at stride 1. So the patent plausibly covers MobileNetV4.
   - timm's Apache-2.0 licence comes from timm's contributors, so it grants no Google patent rights. EfficientNet-B0 and MobileNetV2/V3 face the same issue, so it is not specific to this student. I did not assess it legally.

3. Avoiding segmentation_models_pytorch is a simplicity choice, not a licence necessity. Only some files carry other licences:
   - mix_transformer.py: NVIDIA, non-commercial.
   - mobileone.py: Apple licence.
   - The rest is MIT, BSD-3-Clause or Apache-2.0.

4. The same exclusion covers the ImageNet-12k MobileNetV4 weights, not just ImageNet-1k. For example, mobilenetv4_conv_medium.e180_r384_in12k is tagged apache-2.0 and its card says "Trained on ImageNet-12k by Ross Wightman".

Not checked: the terms of Apple's MobileOne licence, and the Munich GEMA/Suno rulings on memorisation in weights, which I saw in search results only.

licence_checks.what: colour method OpenCV xphoto LearningBasedWB (Cheng et al. 2015)
licence_checks.claim: code: Apache-2.0 (opencv_contrib); weights: The default model ships inside opencv_contrib (Apache-2.0 repo); its training source is not documented; data: The tutorial trains it on Gehler-Shi (https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/modules/xphoto/tutorials/training_white_balance.markdown); the dataset page states no licence (https://www2.cs.sfu.ca/~colour/data/shi_gehler/). Treat as unclear; retrain on your own data if you want it.

verdict.evidence:
Every part of the claim checks out against primary sources. Two points need sharper wording (see corrections).

CODE: Apache-2.0 confirmed.
- The opencv_contrib 4.x LICENSE file is Apache-2.0: https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/LICENSE
- The licence changed from BSD to Apache-2.0 in PR #2628, merged 2020-08-17: https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/pull/2628 . The PR body says: "Many files still contain old-style copyrights though."
- learning_based_color_balance.cpp and white_balance.hpp still carry the old OpenCV 3-clause-BSD "License Agreement For Open Source Computer Vision Library" header (Intel 2000-2008, Willow Garage 2009-2011). Both licences are permissive, so commercial use is fine. Sources: https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/modules/xphoto/src/learning_based_color_balance.cpp and https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/modules/xphoto/include/opencv2/xphoto/white_balance.hpp
- A quick search found no patent on Cheng et al. 2015.

WEIGHTS: shipped in the repo, confirmed.
- The model is modules/xphoto/src/learning_based_color_balance_model.hpp (about 43 KB, compiled in): https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/modules/xphoto/src/learning_based_color_balance_model.hpp
- It has no licence header of its own, so the repo's Apache-2.0 covers it.
- The .cpp uses these built-in arrays when createLearningBasedWB() gets no model path (lines ~100-125). The header documents this: "If not specified, the default model is used".
- The file's only provenance note is: "automatically generated by learn_color_balance.py script using the following parameters: --num_trees 20 --hist_bin_num 64 --max_tree_depth 4 --num_augmented 2 -r 0,0". It names no dataset.
- In the script, "-r 0,0" means all images of the input set: https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/modules/xphoto/samples/learn_color_balance.py
- The model was added in commit 5fbc7daf43 (2016-07-06, PR #736). Commit 75dedf9e58 (PR #747) only renamed identifiers; there was no retraining. Neither commit message, PR body nor PR comments name the training data: https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/pull/736 and https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/pull/747
- "Training source not documented" is therefore literally true.
- However, even the 2016 version of the script says it "Currently supports training only on the Gehler-Shi and NUS 8-camera datasets". Its default ground-truth file is real_illum_568..mat, which is the Gehler-Shi file.

DATA: no licence stated, confirmed.
- The tutorial uses the Gehler-Shi dataset (http://www.cs.sfu.ca/~colour/data/shi_gehler/) and trains on images 0-378 with 30 trees, depth 6 and num_augmented 0. These settings differ from the default model's, so the tutorial does not describe how the default model was made: https://github.com/opencv/opencv_contrib/blob/4.x/modules/xphoto/tutorials/training_white_balance.markdown
- A grep of the raw HTML of https://www2.cs.sfu.ca/~colour/data/shi_gehler/ finds no licence, copyright or terms text. The page only asks you to cite Shi & Funt and Gehler et al. (CVPR 2008).
- The SFU data index (https://www2.cs.sfu.ca/~colour/data/) only thanks Gehler "for permission to post our new versions". That permission was given to SFU; it grants nothing to users.
- The original Gehler page (MPI Tuebingen, archived 2009) also has no licence. It says the work was done during an internship at Microsoft Research Cambridge: https://web.archive.org/web/20090201005215/http://kyb.tuebingen.mpg.de/bs/people/pgehler/colour/index.html
- The NUS 8-camera page also states no licence: https://cvil.eecs.yorku.ca/projects/public_html/illuminant/illuminant.html . The comp.nus.edu.sg link in the script now returns 404.
verdict.corrections:
1) CODE: Better wording is "Apache-2.0 (repo level since OpenCV 4.5.0), with old 3-clause BSD notices still in the LearningBasedWB source files". Keep both notices in the app's third-party credits. Commercial use is fine.

2) WEIGHTS: The script that generated the model only reads Gehler-Shi or NUS 8-camera ground truth, and "-r 0,0" means all images. So the default model was almost certainly trained on the whole of one of those two datasets. Which one is undocumented, and neither dataset states a licence. The weights come from unlicensed academic data, not from an unknown source.

3) DATA: "No licence stated" means no permission is granted (by default all rights are reserved). The data itself is therefore not cleared for commercial use. Only the status of the weights (about 2,400 tree thresholds and leaf values) is legally unclear. Under the project's strict commercial rule, do not ship the built-in model. Pass your own model file via createLearningBasedWB(path).

4) "Retrain on your own data" is not free. Every training photo needs a measured ground-truth illuminant (a grey card or colour checker in the shot), stored in the Gehler-Shi or NUS .mat format the script reads. The owner's existing amateur product photos cannot be used as they are. Labelling them with another auto white balance would only copy that method. The training script needs scipy and scikit-learn, both BSD-3 and fine commercially. GrayworldWB and SimpleWB in the same module use no learned weights and have no data question.

Not checked: the patent search was quick, not exhaustive (two of the paper's authors were at Adobe). opencv.org/license returned 403, so the repo LICENSE file and PR #2628 were used instead.

licence_checks.what: colour method HDRnet (Gharbi et al., SIGGRAPH 2017)
licence_checks.claim: code: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/google/hdrnet/blob/master/LICENSE); TF1/Python 2.7, plus a JAX slicing op; weights: None are available: the README's download.py and pretrained_models are no longer in the repo tree, so you must train your own; data: The repo's training scripts target MIT-Adobe FiveK experts A-E, which is research-only (https://data.csail.mit.edu/graphics/fivek/legal/LicenseAdobe.txt). Train on your own data instead.

verdict.evidence:
VERDICT: The code and data parts hold. The weights part is wrong as stated: pretrained weights do exist and can be downloaded today. They are still not commercially usable, so "train your own" stays right, but for a different reason than the claim gives.

1) CODE is Apache-2.0: CONFIRMED.
- The file https://github.com/google/hdrnet/blob/master/LICENSE matches the official text at https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.txt once whitespace is ignored. GitHub's API also reports it as Apache-2.0.
- The source files carry the header "Copyright 2016 Google Inc. Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0". I checked hdrnet/bin/train.py, hdrnet/models.py, hdrnet/hdrnet_ops.py and jax/bilateral_slice.py.
- The repo is archived (read-only). Its last push was on 2023-04-09. The README says "This is not an official Google product."

2) TF1 / Python 2.7 plus a JAX op: CONFIRMED, with one catch.
- The README says "Tested on Python 2.7, Ubuntu 14.0, gcc-4.8".
- The code only runs on TF1: train.py:108 calls tf.contrib.framework.get_or_create_global_step, models.py:177 calls tf.contrib.layers.convolution2d, and data_pipeline.py:464 uses tf.Session.
- The catch: hdrnet/requirements.txt pins tensorflow_gpu==2.12.0. Dependabot raised it step by step from 1.1.0 (commits 43a11e7, d4d9f37, fccf23f). The tf.contrib code cannot run on that pinned version without porting.
- The JAX slicing op is jax/bilateral_slice.py (Apache-2.0 header). There is also hdrnet/hdrnet_ops_jax_tf2_test.py.

3) WEIGHTS ("None are available"): REFUTED.
- Two things in the claim are true. The master tree of google/hdrnet has no pretrained_models/ folder and no download.py (I fetched the full tree from the API; it was not truncated). The README still refers to both.
- "No longer" is wrong, though: they were never in google/hdrnet. The commits API finds no commit that ever touched pretrained_models. The first commit (e2f1833) does not contain it. The repo's .gitignore excludes the pretrained_models folder.
- The official project page https://groups.csail.mit.edu/graphics/hdrnet/ links "Pretrained models: https://data.csail.mit.edu/graphics/hdrnet/pretrained_models.zip".
- The author's repo https://github.com/mgharbi/hdrnet is the "Code" link on that page. It is an Apache-2.0 fork that contains pretrained_models/download.py, and that script fetches the same zip.
- A HEAD request today returned HTTP 200, application/zip, 235,701,996 bytes, last modified 2017-07-28.
- I read only the zip's index of files (about 256 KB, using an HTTP range request). It holds 138 entries: TF1 checkpoints for experts (experts_cm1, experts_cm2, expertC_comparison), faces, hdrp, local_laplacian (normal_1024, strong_1024), photoshop (6 filters) and style_transfer (1024, 2048, n).
- There is no LICENSE, README or terms file in the zip, and the project page has no licence text. So the weights are available but come with no licence.
- They were also trained on research-only data. The paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.02880, section 4.1.1) says: "Besides HDR+ and the face brightening dataset, all the effects were applied to the unprocessed set of the MIT 'FiveK' dataset". The expert retouches (section 4.2) are MIT-Adobe FiveK as well. Faces come from the Jain & Learned-Miller 2010 dataset.
- The HDR+ model expects 16-bit linear input made from RAW (README), so it does not suit sRGB phone photos anyway.

4) DATA: CONFIRMED.
- scripts/experts/a_nn.sh to e_nn.sh, plus c_highvar50_nn.sh and c_random250_nn.sh, train on data/expert{A..E}/train/filelist.txt. Those are FiveK's five experts. The data itself is not shipped ("data" is in .gitignore).
- The FiveK page https://data.csail.mit.edu/graphics/fivek/ says "You can use these photos for research under the terms of the following licenses". Both licences restrict use:
  - LicenseAdobe.txt covers 2,690 files.
  - https://data.csail.mit.edu/graphics/fivek/legal/LicenseAdobeMIT.txt covers 2,310 files.
  Both are titled "RESEARCH LICENSE" and say "solely for your own research purposes ... not ... intended for or directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation".
- train.py accepts any filelist of input/output pairs (see sample_data/identity), so training on your own data works.

5) PATENT RISK the claim leaves out.
- Google holds US10579908B2, "Machine-learning based technique for fast image enhancement" (inventors Chen, Hasinoff, Gharbi, Barron): https://patents.google.com/patent/US10579908B2/en.
- Google Patents marks it Active, with an estimated expiry of 2037-12-18. The European application EP3602483A1 is listed as Withdrawn. The Chinese one, CN110612549A, is listed as pending.
- All three independent claims (1, 8 and 14) require a mobile device whose image sensor takes the photo and shows the result on its viewfinder.
- A desktop app that processes stored photos looks outside the claims' literal wording.
- The Apache-2.0 section 3 patent licence covers the google/hdrnet code itself. It may not cover a separate PyTorch re-implementation.

Not checked: I did not download the 236 MB zip (I read its file index only) and did not check third-party ports of HDRnet. The patent status is Google's assumption, and none of this is legal advice.
